headline: Percentages are fractions with a common denominator—making comparison effortless
universal_truth: Common standards make comparison possible; without them, we're comparing apples to oranges
fun_facts: The word 'percent' comes from Latin 'per centum'—literally 'by the hundred'
The % symbol evolved from an abbreviation of 'per 100' written as 'p cento' then 'pc' then '%'
Percentages over 100% make sense—200% means twice as much as the original
discussion_questions: Why do we use percentages so much in everyday life?
What's the difference between percentage points and percentages?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: A 20% discount. 78% battery. 95% effective. We're surrounded by percentages because they're brilliantly useful—every percentage uses the same denominator: 100. That common baseline makes instant comparison possible.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Percentages are just fractions out of 100. So why do we use them so much? What makes this particular fraction so universally useful?

options.text: The common denominator of 100 makes any two percentages instantly comparable
options.response: Yes. Comparing 3/4 to 7/9 requires calculation. Comparing 75% to 78% is immediate. Common bases enable comparison.

options.text: 100 is a round number that's easy to work with mentally
options.response: That helps, but the real power is comparability...

q1.title: Universal Standard
q1.script: Before percentages, comparing values was hard. Is 4/7 more than 5/9? Not obvious. But 57% versus 56%? Instantly clear. Percentages convert all fractions to a common scale, enabling rapid comparison.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Universal Standard"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Beyond 100
q2.script: Percentages can exceed 100. A 150% increase means you have the original plus half again. 200% means double. There's no mathematical cap—though in practice, most percentages we encounter are between 0 and 100.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Misleading Math
q3.script: Percentages can mislead. 'Crime up 100%' might mean from 1 case to 2. A drug '50% more effective' sounds impressive until you learn it went from 2% to 3% effective. Always ask: percentage of what?
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Common standards make comparison possible. Percentages teach that shared baselines enable understanding. When comparing anything, first ask: are we measuring against the same scale?
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 103. Tomorrow, we'll explore how we measure things. Until then, notice percentages around you and consider what they're really saying.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Percentage Literacy - Ask 'Of What?'
growTrack.activity: When you encounter a percentage today—in news, advertising, or conversation—ask: percentage of what? What's the base number? A 50% increase from 10 is different from 50% increase from 1,000,000. Context matters.
